definition: In this historical theological context, the rational soul is the specifically human, reasoning part of the soul, contrasted with an animal or irrational soul. In Apollinarianism, the Logos was said to take the place of the human rational soul in Christ.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Apollinarianism; pinned source text

reasons: The packet does not support the claim that “rational soul” is “the specifically human, reasoning part of the soul” contrasted with an “animal or irrational soul.” The packet only states that the human element was reduced to “a body and an animal (or irrational) soul,” and that the Logos took the place of the “human (or rational) soul,” without defining “rational” as a reasoning capacity.

While the second sentence is supported by the packet’s statement that “the Logos took the place of the human (or rational) soul” in Apollinarianism, the first sentence contains an unsupported characterization.
